name: Paman
defining_innovation: The Cape York languages that gave the family the first half of its name (pama 'person'). In the Northern Paman languages, initial consonants were dropped wholesale.

chapters.title: Cape York
chapters.body: The Paman languages fill Cape York Peninsula, close to the probable Pama-Nyungan homeland. They are unusually diverse for a single subgroup. In the far north, the Northern Paman languages dropped the initial consonant of almost every word, a change so drastic that their relationship to the rest was hard to see until **Kenneth Hale** worked it out in the 1960s. The same kind of change happened independently in Arandic.

chapters.title: Kangaroo, and Which Way Is North
chapters.body:
In 1770 James Cook's *Endeavour* spent seven weeks at the mouth of the Endeavour River, where the crew recorded words of Guugu Yimithirr. One of them, *gangurru*, the name of a large grey kangaroo, became the English word 'kangaroo'. The linguist John Haviland later confirmed the word, which had been doubted.

Guugu Yimithirr became famous again in the 1990s. Its speakers describe spatial relations with cardinal directions ('the cup is north of the plate') rather than 'left' and 'right', and research by Haviland and Stephen Levinson showed that they keep track of direction constantly. Wik Mungkan, further south at Aurukun, is still learned by children.

speakers.note: Wik Mungkan (about 950 home users in 2021) and Guugu Yimithirr (about 800) are the largest; many Cape York languages have only a few elderly speakers or none. Census figures count people who use the language at home, including some who are not fully fluent.

sources.citation: Australian Bureau of Statistics. 2022. Census of Population and Housing 2021: language used at home (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages).
Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig, eds. 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.

turning_points.title: Initial dropping
turning_points.description: The Northern Paman languages lose the initial consonant of nearly every word, often along with the first vowel, and weaken the consonants that follow. Hale's reconstruction of these changes was one of the first detailed demonstrations of regular sound change in an Australian language.
turning_points.notation: #C(V) → ∅, with later lenition of the new initial consonant

sources.citation: Hale, Kenneth. 1964. Classification of Northern Paman languages, Cape York Peninsula, Australia: A research report. Oceanic Linguistics 3(2).

turning_points.title: Cook at the Endeavour River
turning_points.description: The crew of the *Endeavour* record Guugu Yimithirr words, including *gangurru*, which enters English as 'kangaroo' and becomes the first Australian word known worldwide.

sources.citation: Haviland, John B. 1974. A last look at Cook's Guugu-Yimidhirr word list. Oceania 44(3).

turning_points.title: Missions and reserves
turning_points.description: Lutheran missions such as Hope Vale, and government reserves, gather speakers of different Paman languages together. English and Guugu Yimithirr become the languages of the missions, and many smaller languages decline.

sources.citation: Bowern, Claire, ed. 2023. The Oxford Guide to Australian Languages. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
